messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 74-year-old female admitted with subcutaneous masses, abdominal pain, and fever.

Clinical course: The patient was admitted with several subcutaneous masses, abdominal pain, and fever. Laboratory tests showed an extremely low platelet count, and serum protein electrophoresis showed a monoclonal band. Imaging studies revealed subcutaneous masses and intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy with moderate splenomegaly. Biopsy of the subcutaneous mass revealed a diagnosis of CSH associated with IgH and Igκ rearrangements, with suspicion of an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder. Further testing of the excised spleen confirmed a diagnosis of DLBCL, non-GCB subtype.

Treatment: The patient underwent laparoscopic splenectomy and was administered eight courses of rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone. The patient was in partial remission 9 months after diagnosis. PET-CT scan showed resolution of some masses, but serum paraprotein levels remained elevated leading to four cycles of rituximab plus lenalidomide, MG is not visible at one-month follow-up.

Outcome: The patient was evaluated and treated for CSH and DLBCL with rituximab and combination chemotherapy. The patient achieved PR with some improvement in PET-CT scans but elevated serum paraprotein levels; treated subsequently with rituximab plus lenalidomide leading to undetectable MG levels. The patient was discharged to the home for follow-up with routine laboratory tests and imaging scans.
Diagnoses: [diagnosis section withheld]

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
Splenectomy confirmed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (non-GCB subtype), and this is the condition chiefly responsible for the admission. The crystal-storing histiocytosis and the monoclonal gammopathy are secondary to it. DLBCL is a malignant neoplasm in chapter C, category C83 (non-follicular lymphoma, C83.3).

CODE: C83
